title: Searching for the Center
author: Terry Underwood
summary: Terry Underwood recounts the 1990s push for national learning standards and authentic assessment, drawing on his own work as a California teacher with Lauren Resnick's New Standards Project. He argues that the project built something genuinely valuable, curriculum-embedded performance tasks and portfolio assessment that put teachers in charge of building, teaching and scoring assessments, before it collapsed in 1996 for lack of time, resources and powerful allies. He uses a jewelry metaphor, cubic zirconium versus diamond, to separate assessment that reflects real classroom learning from curriculum-neutral testing. The post walks through the Man and His Message performance task on Martin Luther King's philosophy of nonviolence as a model of a task worth doing in its own right. It then traces how No Child Left Behind money, Race to the Top, the Common Core and Smarter Balanced pushed states back toward bubble-style testing, and closes by inviting readers to judge a Smarter Balanced performance task against the same standard.
points: Authentic assessment is defined by whether it captures the learning teachers see in living classrooms, not by the reliability of curriculum-neutral tests.
A good curriculum-embedded performance task is itself a unit of instruction that is worth doing in its own right, with evidence of learning collected along the way.
Teachers who write performance tasks need dedicated, in-depth professional development, and building and scoring assessments puts them in the driver's seat.
The New Standards Project collapsed because it could not deliver quickly enough and lacked powerful friends, after which federal funding conditions steered states back to standardized tests.
quotes: Could it be that superior education systems might produce more sophisticated workers who are more valuable in the labor market? Lauren Resnick found that most European countries had created coherent, centered education systems with learning standards, curriculum frameworks, and robust and layered authentic assessment systems.

In classrooms it’s the difference between the learning that teachers see going on in living classrooms when the idea is for children to be learning and the learning somebody would see if they poked in their head for an hour or so with some curriculum-neutral tests. Just as the test is fake (despite its reliability and validity), the learning it measures isn’t the genuine article.

A curriculum-embedded performance task must be worth doing in its own right, since its function is to fit into lesson plans as an instructional unit for a teacher and class with assessment evidence collected and exported for scoring customized to the tasks making up the unit.
Then suddenly, amazingly, in 1996 the NSP collapsed. I heard that the collapse was actually a change in mission and direction. I haven’t a clue about what really happened. It stopped.

For this reason, I argue that teachers who write CEPTs need dedicated, in-depth professional development. They need to understand a good assessment as a precision tool that removes evidence of learning without damage.

The NSP collapsed in 1996 not because it tried to do too much, but because it could not deliver quickly enough. Like CLAS, it needed more time and resources; like Common Core, it needed more friends in positions of power.

But federal dollars from No Child Left Behind as well as Title I money came with standardized assessment strings attached. Many states faced the dilemma of trying to appear assessmentally authentic while holding on to the ease of the bubble test.
